titleEn: [VR Health] Is VR Okay for Kids?
contentEn:
1. Concerns about people's health exist, and there are quite a few concerns about VR. In particular, there are many questions about whether young children can use it, and Oculus warns against use by users under 13, following concerns that it might be dangerous for children whose senses are less developed.

**Is VR too dangerous for kids? We asked the experts** We’ve investigated the age ratings of VR headsets and talked to optometrists and vision experts to find out if VR is safe for children. These are the potential risks of using VR for kids. www.digitaltrends.com

http://www.digitaltrends.com/virtual-reality/is-vr-safe-for-kids-we-asked-the-experts/

However, as seen in the case of Google Expeditions, there are attempts to apply VR in various fields such as education, raising the question of whether it is right to unconditionally prevent young children from using VR.

**Google Expeditions** Imagine exploring coral reefs or the surface of Mars in an afternoon. With Expeditions, teachers can take students on immersive, virtual journeys. www.google.com

https://www.google.com/edu/expeditions/

Furthermore, this issue is very significant as it determines the size of the market, making it a crucial problem.

2. Medical evidence is still lacking, and more time will be needed.

However, no medical 'smoking gun' has yet been found anywhere to prove that VR technology itself is harmful. Even TV... self-illuminating displays have not been around for even a few hundred years in the tens of millions of years of human history. The side effects of this convenience of civilization, which has come to us in a very short time, have not been verified. It takes a considerable amount of time and large-scale statistical tracking to medically determine if something is harmful, but there are no mass-produced products, only a small number of people use it, and the wearing period is limited, so there is a lack of data to accept this as a fact. Further research on this is needed. However, what has been confirmed is that it can cause eye fatigue and photosensitive syndrome, which can also be caused by fluorescent lights and lightning, but this varies greatly from person to person.

{{IMG:1}}

KBS Crisis Escape No. 1 (2011. 08.01)

And there is no medical evidence that the dizziness or discomfort we feel is harmful. Just as no evidence has been found that car sickness or seasickness is harmful to people.

3. Problems will arise when moving between the VR World and the Real World.

You might find it a bit strange that the discussion in this post seems to go back and forth, but long-term VR use could make daily life uncomfortable. Human senses and bodies are highly adaptable, so if they are continuously exposed to abnormal sensory situations like VR, they adapt to them. Later, when returning to normal, there can be a sense of rejection, similar to land sickness or astronauts experiencing 'Earth sickness.' If one is deeply immersed in VR for a long time, it could interfere with daily life. However, this is not significantly different from saying that long periods of living in space or at sea can interfere with life on Earth, and it is questionable whether this is a harm inherent to VR itself. Similar themes have already been depicted in animation, such as the portrayal of prosthetic bodies in Ghost in the Shell, showing the sense of discomfort and sensory confusion when changing bodies, or the child born on the Moon in Planetes who cannot return to Earth.

{{IMG:2}}

From Planetes, Nono at 12 years old

She had the body of an adult to anyone who saw her, but her actual age was 12. As one of the few 'Lunarians' born and raised on the Moon, where gravity is weak, she grew quickly but had weak bone density. She has a congenital low-gravity disorder that prevents her from living in places with strong gravity, so the hospital is her home. - Source: Namu Wiki -

The adaptability of humans and living things is astonishing! Perhaps if we become deeply engrossed in the value that VR offers, we might even evolve with VR. Some might call it degeneration, but then again. (In fact, 'degeneration' and 'evolution' are the same word. Degeneration specifically implies a direction, while evolution should be seen as a higher concept that originally has no direction. Of course, if you argue that the Chinese characters say otherwise, I have nothing to say.)

4. What's more important is the value that the VR World provides.

The reason astronauts go into space, even enduring space sickness and loss of bone and muscle, is because there is value in it. The same applies to VR. No matter how similar VR is made to the Real World, Virtual is Virtual. If it becomes exactly like Real, then Virtual has no value. Therefore, problems, big or small, can arise when returning to the Real World. What is important is the value that Virtual provides. Just as the time we spend on smartphones and PCs increases, and we experience conditions like Turner syndrome or 'turtle neck' syndrome, we use smartphones and PCs because we gain some value from them. Similarly, if we consider VR as an extension, what we should be careful about with VR is using the Virtual World only to the extent that it does not interfere with the Real World. Just as it is healthy not to sit foolishly at a desktop until you can't get up, or not to look at a smartphone until your neck hurts. Additionally, more thorough research should be conducted to ensure that the side effects and fears surrounding VR use are not exaggerated. It seems that efforts are already underway overseas. However, I am concerned that regulations might emerge before the industry even has a chance to grow. **ps. If you have any good additional resources on VR health, please feel free to share links.**

“Manufacturers could build in vision tests and allow people to see that they might have a problem and should consult an eye specialist,” suggests Prof. Banks.

If things go wrong, we might end up buying VR at an optician's...

titleEn: Hydrogen Cars vs. Electric Cars: Electricity Has Already Won
contentEn:
Perhaps because Hyundai is pushing hydrogen, there seem to be an unusually large number of hydrogen proponents in Korea. To be precise, a hydrogen car is a hydrogen fuel cell electric vehicle, but anyway, these two types of cars are not really comparable, yet they seem to be constantly compared, so I'd like to briefly discuss it.

1. Hydrogen Cars Are Essentially Electric Cars in the Research Phase

The ideal of hydrogen cars is good. But in reality, they are not yet usable. To be precise, this thing is merely in the research phase, and its widespread adoption is more difficult and expensive than electric cars. If you complain that electric cars are expensive, you shouldn't even go near hydrogen cars. Electricity is used to produce the fuel, storage is difficult, there's a possibility of explosion, and it leaks easily. There might be a slight advantage in being able to use the existing infrastructure of 12,000 gas stations, but I'm not sure if local residents would be okay with gas stations being converted into hydrogen storage facilities. The conclusion for hydrogen cars is this: if nuclear fusion energy makes electricity so abundant that it's overflowing, then you can decompose water to produce hydrogen and create long-range electric vehicles. To be precise, it's a battery revolution technology, not a technology for changing the car's drive system.

2. The Core of Electric Cars is the End of the Internal Combustion Engine

The biggest change at the core of electric cars is the replacement of the internal combustion engine with a motor. Whether the battery is lithium, a hand-cranked generator, or a hydrogen fuel cell, if it's motor-driven, it's simply an electric car. It has the advantage of being structurally simpler, and electricity is easily convertible into any form. It's difficult to convert gasoline into crude oil, but electricity is easily converted into other forms of energy, and transmission costs are low. You don't have to see fuel tanker trucks driving around, and while there are some efficiency issues, even wireless transmission is possible. This is regardless of whether the power source is thermal or nuclear. The debate that electric cars are not eco-friendly because electricity generation from thermal or nuclear power increases is an energy production issue, not an electric car issue.

3. The Core of Electric Cars is a Paradigm Shift in Charging Infrastructure

Furthermore, the simplest way to implement an electric car is by attaching a battery. This allows for easy control over charging times and enables charging anywhere. This means prices can be raised or penalties applied during peak electricity usage hours, and electricity can be supplied cheaply during off-peak hours when it's abundant. Everyone thinks that if electric cars increase, electricity production must increase accordingly, but in fact, a tremendous amount of nighttime electricity is currently being wasted. This can be used for electric car charging, and in the event of a power shortage, if policies allow, it could even be used as a national emergency battery in reverse. "As a blackout is expected this summer, we will draw nearly 70% of the power from electric vehicles. Those who agree and plug in their vehicles will be compensated for the cost, so you can earn money." Such a policy is possible. This means high efficiency in electricity usage becomes possible. Electric cars can be fast-charged and slow-charged, and in fact, they can be charged anywhere, and the cost of building charging infrastructure is incomparably cheaper than gas stations. All that's needed is an appropriate billing system, and software issues become more prevalent. This is what's meant by the "appliance-ification" and "computerization" of cars.

4. The Market Has Already Decided Towards Electric

Moreover, the market is already moving towards electric. China, the world's largest market, is barely issuing license plates for anything other than electric vehicles, is rapidly becoming the number one country in electric vehicle production, and has set increasing solar power as a policy goal. This strong drive is due to the severe fine dust and various air pollution issues in that region. While some say the Korean government is irresponsible and should demand compensation from China, it's clear that China is also aware of the seriousness and is taking action. In contrast, Korea's policy is lukewarm, and comparing the price and performance of Chinese and Korean electric vehicles, it's no exaggeration to say that Korea has already been caught up. China's 40-seater electric bus has a range of 250km, and its taxis have a range of 415km and a top speed of 140km/h. It's said that they sold 60,000 units worldwide, more than Tesla, but I won't discuss Korean electric vehicles separately.

**10 Facts About China's Electric Car 'BYD' That Surpassed Tesla** It's not an underwear brand. This company is a Chinese electric car manufacturer. And it sold the most electric cars last year. Why not Tesla Motors? Indeed. While Tesla dominated all global media, a Chinese company called BYD quietly increased its market share in the electric vehicle market. Let's uncover all of BYD's secrets today. - BYD Homepage 1. BYD Surpassed Tesla and Nissan [2015 Electric Vehicle Sales Ranking - Green Car Report] In 2015, last year, the company that sold the most pure electric vehicles was not Tesla, which constantly makes headlines, but...
http://thegear.co.kr/12259

Even Europe, home to renowned car manufacturers, with BMW and Volkswagen, is already pushing electric vehicle production, and in the US, GM and Tesla can be considered the originators of electric vehicles. In Japan, only Toyota is still talking about hydrogen, but many companies hold patents for electric vehicles, and Nissan, for example, has sold 50,000 electric vehicles. It seems that Korea, which is most ambiguous in terms of competitiveness for commercial products, is the most passive.

5. Korea Must Stake Its Future on Electric Vehicles.

If we don't develop proper competitiveness, the Korea-China FTA could be poison for the automotive industry. The shipbuilding crisis might be followed by an automotive crisis. Enthusiasts who love internal combustion engines think electric cars are "tasteless" and won't succeed, but for most people, a car is a tiresome money pit. They buy it because they need it, and then, if possible, they buy something cool and good. The latter is difficult to sustain as a competitive advantage. The automotive industry is based on mass production. After all, isn't Hyundai-Kia not primarily a sports car company? Recently, the members who created the electric car Faraday Future came from luxury sports car manufacturing companies. The paradigm has already shifted. Let's not cling to hydrogen; the immediate carbon reduction and fine dust measures we can take are reducing diesel and expanding electric vehicles. The next presidential election will likely see the emergence of a politician who champions the paradigm shift to electric vehicles.

PS. Just in case anyone has expectations for hydrogen... This data is from 2015.

[**undefined** www.energy.or.kr](http://www.energy.or.kr/web/kem_home_new/energy_issue/mail_vol21/pdf/issue_90_05.pdf)

France, 300 units supplied by end of 2015
Germany, 400 charging facilities by 2020
Japan, supply chain established by 2040 (Note: Kurzweil recently moved the singularity from 2045 to 2030)

**Conclusion: Hydrogen cars have not even attempted commercial market penetration yet.**
In contrast, 250,000 electric vehicles were already sold worldwide in 2015 alone.
Hyundai also started selling its compact pure electric car, the Ioniq, and in just a few months, it sold more units than all the hydrogen cars it had ever produced and sold combined. (All previously sold hydrogen cars were for public and research institutions anyway. "Mass production" was just a word.)

titleEn: Ideas for Transitioning to a Hangul-Centric Public Document Environment
contentEn:
1. Purpose of Disclosure

South Korea uses two word processors. One is Hancom Office, used in public institutions and schools, and the other is Microsoft Word, used by the private sector. Recently, Google Docs has also been used, not prioritizing format, and in response, Naver released Naver Word using Synapsoft technology, but it doesn't seem to be gaining traction. Amidst this, the following news article was published, and the reaction from educators I know was, in a word, unenthusiastic. Teachers I know are doing excellent work with Google Docs, collaborating online, and some teachers wonder why the use of specific software is being forced. The advantage and disadvantage of software is that the switching cost is relatively low. Therefore, companies try various methods of lock-in and stake their lives on the quality of their services.

http://news.naver.com/main/read.nhn?mode=LSD&mid=sec&oid=018&aid=0003574358&sid1=001
**Hancom 'Office NEO' Selected as Integrated SW for Gyeonggi Provincial Office of Education** [E-Daily Reporter Jeong Byeong-muk] Hancom (030520) announced on the 28th that 'Hancom Office NEO' has been selected as the integrated office software (SW) for the Gyeonggi Provincial Office of Education. The Gyeonggi Provincial Office of Education... news.naver.com

http://news.naver.com/main/read.nhn?mode=LSD&mid=sec&oid=018&aid=0003574358&sid1=001

However, the actions of the first-generation ventures, whom I deeply respected, are now met with all sorts of criticism. At some point, even though they are in the same software industry, they are almost being called a "software mafia," making me wonder if they have forgotten the fundamental spirit of software – the customer – in their fervent pursuit of their own survival. This corporate survival strategy tends to focus on sales rather than technology, which is poison in the long run. I do not recommend public institution SI projects to capable startups or companies with ample resources. The money the government provides to foster industries is our tax money, meant for companies to grow enough to compete globally, not to cling to these projects. Moreover, the interference is so severe that it doesn't even allow for focusing on the core. A helicopter parent's child lacks competitiveness. How long will they be carried? I particularly do not recommend the use of Hangeul (Hancom Office) for elementary and middle school students. I recommend using Google Docs, even if its features are a bit clunky. The key competencies for future children are collaboration, digital literacy, and global perspective. I feel that Hancom's collaboration support is limited and unstable, and it's not as digitally native as Google Docs. Furthermore, it is detached from global standards. It's difficult to understand why we would hinder the essential competencies children need just to save one company, Hancom. The Ministry of Education should set the most appropriate technology for education and empower the teachers who teach the children. I am now disclosing an idea I had prepared for a proposal some time ago. If things continue this way, the competitiveness of Korean public documents will be nonexistent, and it will be the biggest factor in losing public productivity competitiveness, along with ActiveX. I had written this down purely as an idea to develop the current paradigm and achieve international competitiveness. While it may not be perfect, if implemented with determination by experts, I believe it could bring some competitiveness to this closed environment.

2. Ideas for Improving the Public Electronic Document Environment (First Draft: April 7, 2015)

Existing public document collaboration systems and policies have focused solely on digitizing paper documents. However, in an era centered on software, by developing a collaboration system based on documents that are digital from the creation stage and corresponding policies, we can achieve the values of Government 3.0: sharing, communication, and collaboration.

**□ Current Status and Problems of Public Electronic Documents**

ㅇ **(Closed Technology)** Public documents centered on HWP Hangeul files
- De facto standard use of a specific company's file format (HWP)
- ODF, an international standard, has been selected as a Korean industrial standard, but its use is not mandatory for public institutions.
- Concerns about forcing private companies that collaborate to use a specific company's product (Hangeul word processor).
- Concerns that a specific company's file format (HWP) has low international usage, leading to international isolation.
- ODF, supported by Hangeul and various other word processors, has limitations in actual use due to issues of reproducibility and system integration.

ㅇ **(Web Environment)** Low accessibility and difficulty in searching and sharing
- Public documents are uploaded as files and shared as attachments to specific web posts.
- Attached files are more difficult to search than web documents.
- Due to government security guidelines, the URL of web posts is not disclosed beyond the domain, making it difficult to share and disseminate on SNS sites that typically rely on fixed URLs (Permalinks) for sharing and communication.

ㅇ **(Underutilization)** Limited to use as a substitute for paper documents
- High cost and effort across all stages: creation, distribution, use, circulation, storage, and disposal.
- Advantages such as collaboration and version control are not utilized.
- Failure to achieve a paperless environment.
- Inability to guarantee access due to document changes or deletions.
- In mobile environments, the frequency of using separate document viewers is low, and the small screen size reduces the usability of existing digital documents.

**□ Research Topics for Solutions**

ㅇ **(Open Technology)** Defining and disseminating public document formats
- Defining and disseminating public document file formats considering market impact, global standards, implementability, and usability.
- Establishing a practical technical system through public-private cooperation.

ㅇ **(Web Environment Optimization)** Improving web accessibility and usability of public electronic documents
- Developing SEO strategies optimized for the domestic portal environment.
- Developing web environment improvement strategies for sharing and dissemination (e.g., Permalink).
- Improving accessibility for document changes and deletions.
- Developing mobile response strategies.

ㅇ **(Improving and Disseminating Utilization Environment)** Researching and promoting utilization systems suitable for electronic documents
- Reviewing utilization systems across all stages.
- Developing systems and methods to utilize advantages such as collaboration and version control.
- Analyzing and overcoming obstacles to achieving a paperless environment.

Diagnosis of current status and problems was conducted by dividing into two divisions: citizens and public institutions, to develop integrated improvement plans, which were then pursued as an integrated topic until completion. Irregular individual in-depth interviews were continuously conducted.

ㅇ **(Public Service)** Joint development by two groups: Open Technology and Web Environment Optimization
- **(Open Technology)** Hangeul and Computer, Microsoft, Infraware, Handysoft, Unidocs, Synapsoft, Open Source (OpenOffice) development group
- **(Web Environment Optimization)** Naver, Daum Kakao, Google, Synapsoft, Social Network Expert Group, etc.

ㅇ **(Public Institution Utilization)** Joint dissemination by groups: Open Technology and Utilization Environment Improvement & Dissemination
- **(Open Technology)** Hangeul and Computer, Microsoft, Infraware, Handysoft, Unidocs, Synapsoft, Open Source (OpenOffice) development group
- **(Utilization Environment Improvement & Dissemination)** Korea Electronic Document Industry Association, Web Document Experts, Korea Electronic Document Society, Public Officials, etc.

**□ Expected Effects**

ㅇ **(Establishment of Fair Market Order)** By establishing a document environment compliant with international standards, international compatibility and a fair market order in the document market can be achieved, leading to improved quality through competition in the public document market.
ㅇ **(Improved Job Satisfaction and Productivity)** Maximizing the advantages of digital documents to create a paperless environment will increase job satisfaction within public institutions and enhance productivity.
ㅇ **(Improved Public Satisfaction and Trust)** Creating a digital document environment that enables sharing, communication, and collaboration will improve public satisfaction with digital public documents and enhance trust in the government as a transparent entity.

titleEn: VR All-Purpose Era is Coming: Sports, Education, Military, Industry, Office
contentEn:
This post is a draft manuscript written at the request of the Korea Creative Content Agency (KOCCA). A refined, edited version titled [Zoom 3 The World Expands, Worlds Multiply](http://sitehomebos.kocca.kr/k_content/vol19/vol19_08.pdf) was published in KOCCA's K-Content May/June 2016 issue, "Stimulating the Five Senses: Immersive Content."

http://www.kocca.kr/cop/createcont/view.do?menuNo=200903&nttNo=29
                                [**K-Content < Periodicals < Content Knowledge < Korea Creative Content Agency** www.kocca.kr](http://www.kocca.kr/cop/createcont/view.do?menuNo=200903&nttNo=29)

1. The 2018 PyeongChang Olympics: A VR Olympics

The 2012 London Olympics was a very fast and vivid Olympics for us. People received real-time news about the London Olympics through smartphones, a new medium, and UHD broadcasting began, allowing for a clearer view of the scene. Then, in May 2016, the Ministry of Science, ICT and Future Planning included new ICT technologies in the 2018 PyeongChang Winter Olympics.

{{IMG:1}}
                            .[K-ICT PyeongChang Winter Olympics Realization Strategy, Source: Ministry of Science, ICT and Future Planning]

This is none other than VR (Virtual Reality), which is a hot topic these days. How can virtual reality be integrated into sports where people actually sweat? VR technology makes you feel like you've entered another world through a Head-Mounted Display (HMD). If the London Olympics were watched through a clearer, larger window, the PyeongChang Winter Olympics might allow viewers to wear virtual reality devices like Gear VR and experience being directly at the scene. Technically, this involves filming with 360-degree cameras and then viewing the footage through a VR device. Moreover, it's not only the best seat to watch the game, but you can also turn your head to look for attractive people in the stands. The service model of sports is changing from the concept of one-way broadcasting to providing an on-site experience. Additionally, a better aspect than being physically there is that you can watch comfortably from your sofa at home, and since it's virtual reality, you can also receive additional information like commentary and scores, just as you would on a TV screen. However, for now, VR technology is starting with games and 360-degree videos rather than live broadcasts, as various technical issues still exist. There are various problems such as motion sickness-inducing latency in VR devices and limitations in communication speed for transmitting high-resolution 360-degree videos. The 2018 PyeongChang Olympics is also a testing ground for 5G networks, making it the perfect environment for VR, which requires large-volume data transmission. Thus, the advent of more complete and mature VR technology will enable many more things beyond games and 360-degree videos, such as live sports broadcasts.

2. Cheaper and More Pleasant VR Tourism

What about tourism? In 2018, the same year as the PyeongChang Olympics, Russia will host the World Cup, a global football festival. If you go to Russia, watching the World Cup would be great, but you'd probably also want to visit the Kremlin Palace. However, during your trip, you might very likely encounter unpleasant service, local price gouging, or become exhausted by the bustling crowds.

{{IMG:2}}
                            .[Ideal vs. Reality of Tourist Attractions, Source: Tencent News (騰訊新聞)]

But what if you could experience this with VR? Perhaps that experience would be much more wonderful than reality. You could sightsee closer than reality, in the most magnificent places, and listen to explanations in Korean from a friendly guide. Moreover, the best part about such VR tourism is that it's very inexpensive.

3. Dynamic and Safe VR Educational Content

Furthermore, once you enter the virtual reality world of Moscow, you might have a unique experience that you could never have in the real world. You could visit the magnificent coronation ceremony of Empress Catherine in old Moscow. You would transcend not only space but also time, arriving in the year 1762. Such new experiences have high potential for use in education. Google already launched its Expedition Pioneer program, an educational program using Google's VR device, Cardboard, in September 2015. Within just two months of the program, it provided an environment for 100,000 students to experience over 100 regions around the world, including the Great Wall of China, through virtual reality, rapidly increasing interest in VR-based education.

{{IMG:3}}
                            .[Classroom scene using Cardboard, Source: Google]

Attempts to utilize various digital technologies in education have continuously existed. Children already use word processors for homework and search the internet. Presentations are made using PowerPoint. However, only the medium has changed—paper to word processor, books to the internet, presentations to PowerPoint—the educational experience itself hasn't significantly transformed. VR, however, is highly valuable because it innovates that experience. The experience of putting VR devices on children can have an effect beyond reading books and watching videos. It provides higher immersion than video and offers game-like feedback. Using VR input devices like Oculus Touch, one could conduct science experiments even more safely. There would be no fear of getting burned by an alcohol lamp, and perhaps one could even build a small nuclear reactor. One could visit volcanoes, space, the South Pole, or underwater. While field trips to volcanoes or space might solve the cost issue, no parent would send their child due to safety concerns, but with VR, it's different. Images over text, videos over images, and VR over videos. Finally, with VR technology, educational content has begun to come alive.

4. Industrial and Military Applications of VR

Furthermore, areas where safety is even more crucial are the industrial and military sectors. Many accidents actually occur, and the damage and impact when an accident happens are very significant. It can lead to loss of life or very large financial incidents. Drones or robots equipped with 360-degree cameras could be controlled through VR technology. One could work in dangerous environments without being physically present and without fear of being shot.

{{IMG:4}}
                            .[Norwegian Military's Experiment Securing Virtual Vision with VR, ZDnet]

Moreover, work often involves multiple people collaborating rather than working alone. VR technology can effectively facilitate collaboration, even with people on the other side of the world. Until now, collaboration meant talking with a video camera on, or limited interaction with remote collaboration software like Google Docs. Or, in the medical field, it required very specialized environments like remote surgery. However, VR technology allows for scanning each other's bodies with 3D cameras, enabling multiple people to converse and work together with virtual tools in a virtual room.

{{IMG:5}}
                            .[Microsoft Holoportation, Source: Microsoft Research]

In March 2016, Microsoft unveiled a technology called Holoportation, which turned this imagination into reality. Just like in movies, you can see a distant counterpart in 3D as if they were right next to you. Being together also means being able to do something together. Through this technology, we might be able to escape the discomfort of cramped business class seats.

5. The Meaning of VR

The value VR will offer us in the future is not merely a means for games and videos. Virtual reality technology breaks down the barriers of physical distance and time, which are limitations of the real world. And this technology will be much cheaper than real-world experiences, offering more information and more wonderful experiences. This will change many aspects of our lives and provide new value. Of course, I don't believe VR technology will completely replace reality. It must provide experiences for more senses, not just vision, which is represented by HMDs. Furthermore, it will need to overcome numerous technical limitations. VR has only just begun to show its industrial value and will quickly start to reveal its full potential. And, in the process, I also expect VR to help us discover the value of experiences that VR cannot provide in the real world.

titleEn: Definition and Classification of VR, and 3
contentEn:
While VR is quite hot, I still feel like there's no clear definition for it. The Software Policy Research Institute is interested in VR, and I'm personally trying to organize my thoughts on it, but it seems it will take quite some time for anything concrete to emerge. So, in the meantime, I'd like to share some of my observations about VR.

1. Differences and History of VR and AR

VR and AR show clear differences in terms of technology and user experience. AR is the concept of displaying the real-world situation you're currently seeing and overlaying virtual objects or information on top of it, whereas VR refers to virtual reality. However, these days, there's a tendency to refer to everything as VR, because in its early days, AR meant overlaying 'information' rather than virtual objects. If AR involves drawing virtual objects that don't actually exist in the real world, it actually gets a bit closer to the VR experience. These two actually have slightly different origins: VR aimed to implement virtual game worlds, while AR began in the industrial sector to perform specific tasks better. As a result, VR tends to be more entertainment-oriented, while AR leans more towards being a productivity tool. HoloLens and Magic Leap, which are based on AR but much closer to VR, are also called MR (Mixed Reality). However, having attended today's conference, it seems even foreigners commonly refer to HoloLens and Magic Leap as VR. What's important about dictionary definitions and origins? What matters is how people actually use them. Currently, it can be said that VR and AR capable of drawing virtual objects are collectively referred to as VR. Since virtual objects don't actually exist in the real world, from an explicit standpoint, I believe VR is the correct term.

{{IMG:1}}
Definition of MR (http://goo.gl/A8ykQ7)

Sometimes, AR is described as encompassing VR.

{{IMG:2}}
Definition of MR (http://goo.gl/Sse0fl)

However, I don't agree that AR includes VR. Rather, since AR involves viewing digitally filtered or augmented virtual information, I believe VR is actually a broader concept. While there might be some debate on this point, given that VR is emerging as the overarching term, I wonder if historically AR and VR existed separately, then AR's successor became MR, and now everything is being integrated under the term VR. If I had to draw a diagram, it would look something like this:

{{IMG:3}}
Recent Definition of VR

2. Who will win between Vive and Oculus? Actually, they are different devices.

When discussing VR, people often ask which will dominate the market more: Oculus or HTC Vive. Additionally, HoloLens and Magic Leap, set to be released in the second half of the year, are also of great interest. However, in my opinion, these two devices are completely different. It's like asking, 'Can the iPad beat the Galaxy S?' Because these devices require different user behaviors in entirely different spaces. Therefore, I've summarized the aforementioned VR and AR collectively as follows:

{{IMG:4}}
Classification of VR Products from a User Perspective (My Own Classification)

The biggest technical divergence between VR and AR, from a user's perspective, might be whether they see the real world, but from a technical standpoint, the key focus is slightly different.

1) VR

VR is a system where there's increased interest in user behavior, such as whether the user is sitting, where they are looking, if they tilted their head, or wiggled their fingers.

1.1) Seating

Devices like Oculus and PlayStation VR, which largely assume a seated user, are suitable for games and 360-degree videos. They would be suitable for typical 'lean-back' content or RPG games that require a comfortable posture for extended periods.

1.2) Standing

As briefly mentioned earlier, HTC Vive is difficult to see as a competitor to Oculus. These devices, which require a specific space and assume the user is standing, demand quite active engagement. Such games already existed with Kinect and Wii. They are suitable for arcade-style games, as they require a space of a few meters and demand full-body movement from the user. Suitable for arcade-style VR rooms.

1.3) Mobile

Mobile VR, represented by Samsung Gear VR and Cardboard, doesn't just mean plugging in a smartphone. The reason smartphones are currently plugged in is because it's cheap. If standalone devices become cheaper, mobile devices that don't require a smartphone will also emerge. More importantly here is portability. These are devices that can be easily moved and enjoyed for short periods anywhere. Such VR devices are suitable for educational purposes. Of course, if mobile devices could also do motion tracking and 3D rendering at Oculus's level, they might take over everything else, but considering that laptops still haven't overtaken desktops, it's highly likely that this market will remain separate.

2) AR

The biggest difference of AR compared to the aforementioned VR is that it uses more processing power not only for what the user's body is doing but also for scanning the surroundings. In the case of HoloLens, it uses quite a bit of processing just to scan its surroundings, recognize 3D space, and drop virtual objects. AR used for industrial purposes will be a device that focuses more on speed and scanning its surroundings rather than requiring high-resolution graphics, as it's crucial to achieve its specific objectives in real-time. Therefore, it's technically difficult to expect AR to completely supersede VR.

2.1) Outdoor

A prime example of outdoor AR is Google Glass. Outdoors, displaying content under sunlight is an issue, so brightness and battery life will be significant concerns. In the case of Google Glass, experiencing it revealed it wasn't really a usable product. However, the industrial value of outdoor AR is immense. Among them, the defense industry will hold the largest position. Even more so in Korea, where a 1 million won item can be supplied for 100 million won.

2.2) Indoor

Indoor AR has a high potential to develop into productivity tools and educational devices. Wearing a VR device in an office is practically very inconvenient because you can't see your colleagues. It might be perfectly possible just by viewing the outside through a camera on a VR device, like Video Through. However, conceptually, such VR devices can be classified under AR, so for now, I can put them in AR. Therefore, rather than classifying by specific device, I've separated indoor AR from a user experience perspective.

2.3) Transport

Mobile devices like cars, airplanes, and buses have high potential for AR utilization. For this reason, many related companies are traditional automotive manufacturers. Perhaps if autonomous cars emerge and eliminate driving altogether, it might be different, but for now, windows will exist, and there might be a desire to see information about the surroundings. And it goes without saying that its potential for military use is high. A fighter jet's HUD is a prime example of a mobile AR device.

3. 360-degree video as VR's best killer content, or rather, an introductory content.

Personally, I cannot agree with the claim that 360-degree video is the best VR content. 360-degree video is one type of video that can be experienced with VR devices. And strictly speaking, 360-degree video is not VR. Because it lacks the virtual value of 'virtual'. One could even say that adding speech bubbles in AR is closer to VR. It would be more accurate to view 360-degree video as an extension of 4K and 8K. Therefore, saying that 360-degree video is everything in VR is actually absurd, and I don't believe the success or failure of 360-degree video will affect the VR game market. Just as 4K movies didn't affect the high-resolution 3D gaming market. The two are strictly different markets. VR is a computing environment, like computers or mobile devices. When mobile devices emerged, map services and video services appeared, but neither of them overwhelmed the other. They are simply services in different domains. Therefore, I don't think they need to compete. However, what concerns me a bit is the excessively high interest in 360-degree video, and I believe the reasons are as follows:

1) Ease of Production and Distribution

360-degree videos are easier to produce than games. It's a matter of quality, but in any case, after purchasing a special camera, content can be created with just actors, and compared to other VR content with fragmented distribution platforms, powerful major platforms like YouTube and Facebook exist.

2) New Growth Engine for Broadcasting and Telecommunications

The largest sector of IT in South Korea is broadcasting and telecommunications. There are many policies related to this sector, and it actually generates a lot of money. There's a high demand for new growth engines, and from a broadcasting perspective, 360-degree video is a new endeavor; from a telecommunications perspective, VR video is an excellent source for generating more communication fees and the best item for 5G expansion. In fact, due to these points, 360-degree video tends to have a strong supplier-driven push.

3) Ease of Applying Famous IP and Adult Content

One of the easiest ways to attract users in content is through the fame of existing content. Famous celebrities, popular characters, and another is adult content that seeks new experiences and stimulation. 360-degree video is in the best position to apply these elements.

4) Proliferation of Mobile VR

VR devices, the only one that's somewhat widely adopted is Gear VR, and even more widely adopted is Cardboard, which costs less than 10,000 won. At this price point, the only experience it could offer was turning your head 360 degrees. Very few people have even used Cardboard's magnetic button, let alone attached a Bluetooth gamepad to Gear VR. In this situation, 360VR is the only easily accessible option. However, as mentioned earlier, 360-degree videos lack the most important value that VR possesses: the value of "Virtual." The China VR Industry White Paper discusses three values of VR: immersion, imagination, and interaction. 360-degree videos only utilize immersion among these VR values. The added value of imagination and the interaction component are absent. I believe the video below, which adds the value of imagination as VR, is closer to true VR than a typical 360-degree video that simply records a performance as is. (For those who find dry text difficult to read, I've attached a soft, imaginative video to stimulate your imagination.)

A market for typical 360-degree videos like dramas, sports, and performances will exist. It might even replace the TV or 4K video market, and that market is not small. I like games, but these days I also enjoy lying on the sofa and watching IPTV. However, it's a clear reality that this does not provide all the values that VR offers, and I expect it will certainly be highly effective as an introductory content for users who want to experience all these VR values. However, it seems that even current 360VR has not yet discovered the full value that 360-degree videos can offer. Even the novelty of turning around to look behind you in a 360-degree video quickly wears off, and expecting users to replay it just because they missed something behind them shows a profound lack of understanding of users. How many enthusiasts do you expect will watch a movie two or three times, or play a game to the ending two or three times? Therefore, from the perspective that I hope the view on VR broadens, I am wary of only talking about 360VR.

4. A more detailed report to come

This post is my independent summary based on observing VR and AR technologies over time. Assuming the VR technology framework described above, there's an endless amount to research regarding what technologies are needed in each industry sector, and what the situations are like in Korea and abroad. New technologies and content are pouring out faster than expected, almost daily. Based on this, I plan to conduct research and write a more proper report, but since I don't know when it will be ready and timeliness is important, I'm publishing this light version. **Also, I'd like to hear if there are any parts that this framework is missing, and to gather opinions from various experts. (Comments are welcome)** I even wonder if we are in the process of establishing the very concept of VR, given the sheer variety of technologies being called VR.

titleEn: Modular Phone Google Ara Is Different From G5
contentEn:
1. Modular Phones as the New Trend in Smartphones?

Looking at articles about modular phones in Korea, it feels like modular phones are being treated as the new trend in smartphones. It feels like modular phones are simply seen as expandable phones where users can choose their preferences. However, I was quite shocked when I saw Google Ara's project. This might be the first signal of Google shedding its long-standing image as a software company. Whatever the architecture of the Android phone Google created as a reference, it was essentially a lightweight Linux desktop machine with some phone functionalities added. In terms of computer architecture, not much has fundamentally changed. The PC's power supply was replaced by a battery, the monitor by IPS or AMOLED, and the keyboard and mouse by capacitive touch. Honestly, it's a machine no different from a computer. In contrast, Apple's image as a hardware powerhouse didn't originate with smartphones. Apple's hardware prowess, which dates back to early Apple, involves technologies found in computer science textbooks.

2. But the Ara Concept is Post-Smartphone, Not Just New

But Ara is different. Google isn't just talking about a slightly different, smaller desktop-like smartphone; it's talking about a modular hardware computing environment.

{{IMG:1}}
                                
                            http://www.modularphonesforum.com/news/project-ara-15-questions-and-answers-2214/

It's like applying today's distributed software technology to hardware. Indeed, the best insights seem to come from developers, not news articles. I'm just puzzled why reporters don't grasp how significant this is.

[**- YouTube** YouTube에서 마음에 드는 동영상과 음악을 감상하고, 직접 만든 콘텐츠를 업로드하여 친구, 가족뿐 아니라 전 세계 사람들과 콘텐츠를 공유할 수 있습니다. youtu.be](http://www.youtube.com/embed/F3S6Kjb3m0g)

" " All modules can generally support any function, allowing for various operations across different form factors. Future frames can be larger, or smaller. It will be a device completely different from a smartphone. " A technical look reveals that it supports variable power supply, a very fast low-power data bus (UniPro network), an application-independent software stack, and Graybus, among others. Its speed allows for real-time 4K video transmission between modules, using only about 1/3 of the power of USB. The features immediately noticeable to users are multiple slots and the ability to expand functionality without rebooting. Currently, there are 6 slots... but theoretically, it's possible to do something like the 108-robot combination shown below. Surely some idle developer might create this with Ara... The Ara platform would definitely be useful for building a 108-combination robot. (Ara was soliciting ideas, should I submit one?)

3. The G5 is Expandable, Not Modular.

So, what about the G5? Let's look at the nostalgic Space Three Musketeers. (Couldn't find the Korean version)

The Space Three Musketeers don't combine or fuse. Of course, there are terrifying cartoons where living beings combine, but... what's even more regrettable is that the G5 has only one module, and a look at the AppsPortTM 1.0 spec reveals it's USB 2.0. There are clear limitations in speed and power. Moreover, it requires a reboot, which means it has the disadvantage of not being attackable during its transformation time.

4. Google's Ara is a Distributed Hardware Module Form Factor.

I'm certain that Ara is not a phone meant for immediate sale. Let's stop comparing it to the G5. They are completely different devices. While it might look like garbage commercially right now, technologically, it's a phone beyond comparison. It's closer to a device created by a research organization aiming to capture future computing technology, rather than a phone made by marketing and product planning departments like LG's. The difference between the G5 and Ara is as vast technologically as the gap between a smartphone and a feature phone. Comparing the two is absurd in itself. And the technology used to create Ara is quite useful. I believe it could become a pretty good platform for IoT in the future.

1. VR. Of course, porn will work.

When talking about the VR market, a joke often comes up: "Wouldn't the adult content market be easy?" And recently, I heard news that an adult VR content event in Japan was a great success.

However, I find these reactions uncomfortable. I get the impression that "adult content" is like a fruit we could easily pick, but we are too noble to do so, and that Japanese people are being portrayed as primitive perverts. But I confess, I have encountered quite a bit of Japanese adult content. Even at a relatively young age, I knew content from companies like Elf and Illusion, which have recently gone bankrupt one after another. And I've also come across doujin games and doujinshi created by Japanese amateurs.

I also heard that for VR filming of female singers, low angles are insisted upon. Simply put, this indicates that the commodification of sex is happening in Korea just as much as in Japan. The consumption rate of adult content in Korea is already a given, and everyone knows that the adult market exists, even if it's not legally recognized. Even I, who has never been to such places, know where they are.

3. Not to point out the commodification of sex, but to look at it properly.

I'm not trying to say that I'm actually against the commodification of sex. The commodification of sex is not just about packaging female sexuality, as feminists claim. Numerous sexual codes are processed and sold to both women and men. Almost everything we know contains sexual codes, directly or indirectly. Sexual codes are not as simple as most people think.

http://www.slideshare.net/yonghakim900/ndc-2014
                                **[NDC 2014] Moe Theory** In the East Asian subculture scene, 'Moe (萌え)' is a representative concept referring to attractive characters. What is 'Moe'? What kind of character can be considered 'Moe'? How to create a 'Moe' character? This slide presents a new perspective on 'Moe' through various examples. www.slideshare.net

http://www.slideshare.net/yonghakim900/ndc-2014

In fact, the bigger problem, in my opinion, is that Korea is ignorant and has a low understanding of sexual culture and expression, to the extent that the idea that men are weak to visual information is used in school sex education materials.

{{IMG:2}}
                                
                            Did the people who made this learn about sex from pornography and create this material?

Because of this, there's a feeling that expectations for adult content in Korea are either excessively high or excessively disparaged. Adult content is still content. Content has various codes, changes, and is consumed. The belief that unconditional strong stimulation will be effective is on the level of the Ministry of Gender Equality and Family, which treats games as addictive substances. Actual content creators know very well that unconditional stimulation is not effective.

4. The reason I envy Japan is the cultural diversity that comes from lifting taboos and bringing things into the open.

The reason I envy Japan's adult content market, at least, is that there are so many diverse codes and strata, and the consumer base is visible enough to allow for discourse on it.

{{IMG:3}}
                                
                            The simplest example of a heroine... In fact, adult content is more diverse.

Therefore, Japanese sexuality is rich and can exist freely in other content. In old Korean movies, showing a beach as a metaphorical expression, if you think about it differently, how comical is that? A certain manga I encountered as a flash doujinshi in college had subtle ambient sounds with each page turn. The splashing sound of pool water, the sound of wind... The very effects you can feel in Naver webtoons today were being used in Japanese doujinshi when I was in college. Of course, there were H-scenes, but the direction was so fresh that it was shocking to me, and it was sufficient as a preliminary direction to beautifully depict the H-scenes. Thinking back, it had a bit of a Makoto Shinkai vibe, perhaps? And Japan's advantage is that such an adult doujinshi market, as a paid market, greatly helps creators in their free creation. While Lezhin Comics occupies a position for adult content and some content is somewhat precarious, the scope of expression has expanded beyond just being explicit adult material to various other fields. In some Middle Eastern countries, holding hands can be a sexual code, while in some tropical countries, exposing one's chest might not be a sexual code. In fact, the degree of stimulation and the code's impact are determined by the consumer group and the direction. Something can be not explicit at all but appear sexual through direction, and something explicit can evoke no arousal and different emotions due to direction. Simply put, many women feel uncomfortable with explicit content watched by men, but in fact, male viewers might also feel uncomfortable with female-oriented content. So, I'm not saying we should eliminate and despise both for each other's sake. The important thing is to acknowledge diversity, understanding that appropriate content can be consumed by appropriate audiences, and that it might be uncomfortable for other groups. I believe this is a good way to preserve cultural diversity. Of course, crime is another matter. In other words, we don't need to disparage Japanese adult content, and it's not as easy a market as one might think, as adult content is still content. Rather, I believe that because Korea consumes adult content illicitly, disregarding copyright, situations arise where content and reality cannot be distinguished, and proper adult content is not valued.

5. Adult content is not easy, and VR is no different.

My opinion is the same for VR. Immersion is important in adult content, but what actually creates that immersion is not whether it's 2D or 3D. If that were important, people wouldn't react to comics or graphics. The strength of comics and graphics lies in imagination. Immersion comes from imagination, not realism. Imagination is maximized through story and direction, not from UHD video where you can see every blemish on an actress. The same applies to VR. VR adult content is likely to be more restricted in storytelling than in display. Just as VR games are experimental, VR adult content also requires much experimentation. Of course, VR adult content, being advantageous for curiosity, might be good for attracting users. However, I'm still not sure if it will save VR. How many people would buy a million-won device just to watch realistic pornography? It might serve as a means to attract curiosity, but I doubt it will save VR. I believe something more than sexual curiosity that continuously requires VR needs to be created.

6. Let's view VR as a technology that comforts humans.

Virtual sex is, in fact, a connection with lonely people, and VR is the value of virtual space. Thinking a bit more broadly, not just erotic sex but also platonic love is suitable for VR, and VR games and many other content will try to explore these elements. Unlike AR, you can't see the person next to you in VR. And you can't see that you're alone either... I hope that VR technology can connect many lonely people to the world and bring them comfort. titleEn: The Real Smart Thermometer for Kids, Thermocare is Good for Newborns
contentEn:

What could it be?

                                [**[Thermocare] A smarter and safer thermometer than the Braun thermometer** 1. Do you know the Braun thermometer? A thermometer that every home with a child has, the Braun thermometer... blog.naver.com](http://blog.naver.com/fstory97/220559178208)

1. A smart thermometer in my hands

The smart thermometer I participated in crowdfunding for last December has arrived.

{{IMG:2}}

{{IMG:3}}

2. First impression: It's pretty.

My first impression is that it's pretty. It's much prettier than the bulky Braun thermometer I have at home. It's designed to fit well in a woman's hand, and the grip feels good. It uses two standard AA batteries, so they're easy to replace, and there are three buttons in total. While a smart thermometer is typically used in conjunction with a smartphone, it works perfectly fine on its own and its basic functions are surprisingly robust.

3. Measurement is easy and fast.

Measurement method: Point it at the child's forehead or temple area and press the middle button. Above all, I was surprised by how incredibly fast the measurement speed is. The button flashed briefly, and then it displayed the temperature. Since it's a non-contact thermometer, there were slight differences depending on where it was measured, but not to a significant degree. It felt like I could take 5 or more measurements in the time it takes to take about 2 measurements with a standard in-ear Braun thermometer.

4. Easy to measure at night.

Children often get fevers at night, and my role then was to shine a phone light. It required a two-person team: my wife measuring and me illuminating. If the strong phone screen light even slightly shone on the child's face, I'd usually get scolded. However, a feature of Thermocare is that it's easy to measure at night. This is because it displays with an LED. Watch the video below. (It's normal not to see much; the flashing light at the end is the measurement result.) Let's not disturb a child's deep sleep. They say it hinders growth... which is a very important issue for me.

{{IMG:4}}

5. Surprisingly useful object temperature measurement

After moving recently, a slight inconvenience arose: my apartment uses an individual boiler, and if I turn on the bathwater, it gets excessively hot. Pressing the top-left button changes the icon from a person to a box. The box indicates object temperature measurement mode.

{{IMG:5}}
                                
                            Press lightly

{{IMG:6}}
                                
                            Into object measurement mode like this

{{IMG:7}}
                                
                            Bathwater starts running, lukewarm temperature

It's a bit cool. A bit too cold for kids to bathe in.

{{IMG:8}}
                                

https://blog.naver.com/PostView.naver?blogId=fstory97&logNo=223833999385&redirect=Dlog&widgetTypeCall=true&noTrackingCode=true&directAccess=false#

{{IMG:9}}
                                
                            It's gotten a bit warmer. A good temperature for bathing.

{{IMG:10}}
                                

https://blog.naver.com/PostView.naver?blogId=fstory97&logNo=223833999385&redirect=Dlog&widgetTypeCall=true&noTrackingCode=true&directAccess=false#

{{IMG:11}}
                                
                            Ugh... I knew it was hot, but it's over 55 degrees Celsius.

It was hot even with rubber gloves on when washing dishes, so there was a reason. It's also possible to measure baby bottle temperatures as an example. When measuring object temperatures, it's best to align the measurement sensor with the object you want to measure. Since it's non-contact, if you don't pay attention, you might measure a completely wrong spot. Also, the measurement temperature range is 10 to 70 degrees Celsius, so it's inaccurate for industrial uses like measuring a blast furnace or a refrigerator. Please keep this in mind.

6. Smartphone integration

As a smart thermometer, smartphone integration is a given. By connecting via Bluetooth, you can do this... and add family members for individual measurements.

{{IMG:12}}

You can delete incorrect measurements. The 27.8-degree reading was just an air measurement. Temperatures outside the normal range seem to be indicated with a different color... Huh? A new discovery: the app also displays temperature and humidity. Haha, since the appropriate humidity varies with temperature, this information seems very useful. Additionally, it provides various health and hospital information, allowing for immediate response based on the child's condition. Currently, the app is in its early version and feels a bit unstable, but they plan to improve it quickly, so it's worth looking forward to. Apple HealthKit is currently being integrated, and Samsung S Health and Google Fit will be supported sequentially.

7. A smarter AI smart thermometer

Even with just this much, it seems to be worth buying, but even better news I heard from M-Tree Care, who is developing Thermocare, is that the service will become even smarter in the future by utilizing artificial intelligence.

{{IMG:13}}
                                
                            Source: 4th ICT-A.I Forum, Reliability Study on Pediatric Febrile Patient Response Using Thermocare Smart Thermometer and IBM Watson

No joke, they are creating an AI thermometer using IBM's AI Watson, which has beaten humans in quiz shows and performs cancer diagnoses beyond the level of doctors. Wow. Even though a thermometer might seem like nothing, as a medical device, it requires high reliability and undergoes numerous verifications. And it aims for more effective treatment and care based on data. While it will start as a simple temperature measurement device, I expect it to evolve into a service that acts like an AI family doctor in the future. And the fact that this is possible just by a software upgrade to a device purchased once, isn't that great? Instead of having to buy a new device every time a new feature comes out, I support the Thermocare thermometer that will automatically evolve into a better service. Moreover, in a situation where high-quality, low-cost devices from China are flooding the market, it seems like a good IoT device that competes on quality, capability, and reliability.

8. General sale not yet. Special limited sale scheduled for June 13th on 11th Street.

Ah... Lastly, many people ask about where to buy it, but it's not available yet. The general sale price will be 69,900 won through 11th Street on June 13th. As a little extra buying tip, it will be sold for 55,900 won for a limited quantity of 500 units, so those planning to buy should take advantage of this. If you're planning to buy a Braun thermometer or any other thermometer, I recommend holding off for a bit. **P.S.
